songInfo.title: Riptide
songInfo.key: C Major (Am shapes, Capo 1 = Db Major)

keyAndScale.primaryKey: C major (open shapes with capo 1; sounding key Db major)

scalesUsed.notes: C - D - E - F - G - A - B - C (sounding Db - Eb - F - Gb - Ab - Bb - C - Db with capo)
scalesUsed.application: All chords and melodies derive from the C major scale using open chord shapes

scalesUsed.notes: A - B - C - D - E - F - G - A
scalesUsed.application: The progression starts on Am, giving the song a minor feel despite being diatonic to C major
Vocal melody primarily uses pentatonic notes for its catchy, singable quality

keyAndScale.modalCharacter: Aeolian-influenced Ionian (starts on vi chord giving a minor feel within a major key)
keyAndScale.keySignature: No sharps or flats (C major shapes; with capo 1, sounding key has 5 flats)
keyAndScale.relativeMinor: A minor (the song begins on Am, emphasizing the relative minor)

mainProgression.description: One of the most common pop progressions in music, starting on the relative minor (Am) giving a slightly melancholy feel that resolves through the major chords

sectionProgressions.description: The same four-chord pattern repeats throughout the verse with a steady strumming pattern
Same progression continues through the pre-chorus with slight dynamic increase
The chorus uses the identical progression with more energetic strumming and vocal intensity

harmonicFunction: Am (vi) - Relative minor; starting on vi gives the progression a bittersweet, minor-tinged character
G (V) - Dominant chord providing forward motion toward the tonic C
C (I) - Tonic major chord; the arrival point that provides resolution and brightness
F (IV) - Subdominant creating gentle harmonic tension that cycles back to Am
The entire song uses the same four chords in the same order - simplicity is the key
This vi-V-I-IV pattern is closely related to the I-V-vi-IV pop progression, rotated to start on vi

techniques.name: Basic Strumming Pattern
techniques.description: A consistent down-up strumming pattern that drives the entire song, requiring steady rhythm and the ability to maintain the pattern through chord changes

notes: Basic pattern: Down-Down-Up-Up-Down-Up (D-D-U-U-D-U)
This 16th-note based pattern creates the song's rhythmic drive
Accent the first downstroke of each chord change
Keep the strumming hand moving in a constant pendulum motion
Even when 'missing' a strum on muted beats, the hand keeps moving
sequence: Start with the Am chord and establish the strumming pattern
Maintain the pattern through the change to G
Continue through C and F without breaking rhythm
Loop the four-chord cycle with consistent strumming
Add dynamics by varying strum intensity in different sections
tips: Keep your strumming arm moving like a pendulum even during rests
Practice the strum pattern on muted strings before adding chords
Don't grip the pick too tightly - a relaxed grip creates a better sound
Tap your foot on beats 1 and 3 for steady timekeeping
Start slowly and only increase speed once the pattern is automatic

techniques.name: Capo Usage
techniques.description: Using a capo on the 1st fret to transpose the open chord shapes up a half step without changing fingering, matching the original recording's key

notes: Place capo on the 1st fret, centered between the nut and fret wire
The capo should apply even pressure across all 6 strings
Check each string for buzzing after placing the capo
Open chord shapes remain the same; all pitches sound a half step higher
Am shape sounds as Bbm, G shape sounds as Ab, C sounds as Db, F sounds as Gb
sequence: Place capo on 1st fret with even pressure
Play each string individually to check for buzzing
Adjust capo position if any strings are muted or buzzing
Form the Am chord and strum to verify clean sound
Play through all four chords to confirm tuning stability
tips: Place the capo close to the fret wire (but not on it) for best intonation
Spring-loaded capos are easiest for beginners
If strings go slightly sharp after capo placement, that is normal - slight retuning may help
The song can also be played without a capo in the key of C (just lower by a half step)
Capos are essential tools for matching keys to vocal ranges

techniques.name: Simple Open Chord Shapes
techniques.description: The four open chord shapes used in Riptide (Am, G, C, F) are among the most fundamental guitar chords, making this an excellent song for learning chord transitions

notes: Am: X-0-2-2-1-0 (open A string, 2nd fret D and G, 1st fret B, open high E)
G: 3-2-0-0-0-3 (3rd fret low E, 2nd fret A, open D-G-B, 3rd fret high E)
C: X-3-2-0-1-0 (3rd fret A, 2nd fret D, open G, 1st fret B, open high E)
F: X-X-3-2-1-1 (simplified - 3rd fret D, 2nd fret G, 1st fret B and high E)
Alternatively use Fmaj7: X-X-3-2-1-0 if full F barre is too difficult
Focus on getting clear notes from each string in every chord
sequence: Learn each chord shape individually and strum to check all notes ring clearly
Practice switching Am to G (lift fingers, reposition, strum)
Practice switching G to C (keep ring finger on 3rd fret as pivot)
Practice switching C to F (this is often the hardest transition for beginners)
Chain all four: Am - G - C - F at a slow tempo
tips: Press strings with the fingertips, not the flat of the finger
Position fingers close to the fret wire for clearest tone
If F is too hard, substitute Fmaj7 (lift the high E string finger) or play a partial F
Use common fingers between chords as anchors during transitions
The G to C transition shares the ring finger on the 3rd fret - use it as a pivot
details.progression: Am - G - C - F (open chord shapes)

sections.name: Intro
sections.description: Brief guitar intro establishing the strumming pattern and four-chord progression before the vocals enter
notes: Establish the strumming pattern from the very first beat
Light, bouncy strum appropriate for the indie pop feel
Set the tempo and groove before vocals enter
Capo on 1st fret throughout

sections.name: Verse 1
sections.description: First verse using the Am-G-C-F progression with steady strumming at a moderate dynamic level to support the conversational vocal style
notes: Maintain a moderate strumming volume to leave room for vocals
Keep the strumming pattern consistent through chord changes
The chord change happens on beat 1 of every 2 measures (approximately)
Relaxed, easy feel - don't overthink it

sections.name: Pre-Chorus
sections.description: Pre-chorus building slightly in energy with the same chord progression but increased strumming intensity leading into the chorus
notes: Slightly increase strumming intensity
Same progression and pattern as verse
Build energy naturally toward the chorus
The dynamic lift comes from strumming harder, not faster

sections.name: Chorus
sections.description: Full-energy chorus with the same four chords strummed more vigorously, providing the rhythmic foundation for the catchy vocal hook
notes: Full strumming energy for the chorus
Same four chords in the same order
The dynamic contrast between verse and chorus comes from strumming intensity
This is the most energetic section - commit to strong, confident strumming

sections.name: Verse 2
sections.description: Second verse returning to moderate dynamics with the persistent Am-G-C-F cycle
notes: Pull back dynamics to verse level
Maintain the same strumming pattern consistently
The repetition is intentional - the song's charm is in its simplicity
Focus on clean chord transitions

sections.name: Final Chorus and Outro
sections.description: Final chorus repeated with full energy, followed by a brief outro where the strumming fades on a final Am chord
sections.progression: Am - G - C - F - Am (final resolution)
notes: Full energy chorus as the song winds toward its conclusion
The final repetitions may have slight variations in vocal melody
Song ends on an Am chord - the relative minor provides a bittersweet close
Let the final Am chord ring out

guitar.recommended: Acoustic guitar (any steel-string dreadnought or concert body)
alternatives: Ukulele (the original instrument for this song)
guitar.pickup: Acoustic or clean electric tone; no distortion needed

amp.recommended: Acoustic amp or PA system (for acoustic guitar); if electric, any clean-channel amp
alternatives: Any practice amp on clean channel
Direct into an audio interface for recording

effects.reverb: Light room reverb for natural ambience
effects.other: Capo on 1st fret required to match the original key

beginner.focus: Learn the four basic open chords and a simple strumming pattern
steps: Learn the Am chord shape and strum to check all strings ring clearly
Learn the G, C, and F (or Fmaj7) chord shapes individually
Practice transitioning between Am-G, G-C, and C-F slowly
Learn a simple down-strum pattern (all downstrokes on quarter notes)
Play through the four-chord cycle with quarter-note strums

intermediate.focus: Master the strumming pattern and play the song from start to finish
steps: Learn the D-D-U-U-D-U strumming pattern on muted strings
Apply the strumming pattern to each chord individually
Combine the strumming pattern with chord changes at slow tempo
Practice playing along with the recording at full tempo
Add dynamic contrast between verse and chorus

advanced.focus: Sing while playing and add stylistic embellishments
steps: Practice the strumming pattern until it is fully automatic
Add the vocal melody while maintaining the strum pattern
Experiment with muted strums and ghost strokes for rhythmic variety
Try fingerpicking variations for a softer dynamic contrast
Perform the complete song confidently for an audience

commonMistakes: Stopping the strumming hand during chord changes instead of maintaining the pendulum motion
Gripping the pick too tightly, creating a tense and stiff strum sound
Struggling with the F chord and getting frustrated - use Fmaj7 as a substitute
Playing all sections at the same volume without dynamic contrast
Forgetting to place the capo on the 1st fret when trying to play along with the recording
practiceRoutine: Warm up with 2 minutes of strumming open strings using the D-D-U-U-D-U pattern
Practice each chord transition in isolation for 2 minutes each (Am-G, G-C, C-F, F-Am)
Play through the four-chord cycle with the strum pattern at 80 BPM for 5 minutes
Increase tempo gradually to 102 BPM (full song tempo)
Play along with the original recording from start to finish
focusAreas: Clean chord transitions without pausing between changes
Consistent strumming pattern (D-D-U-U-D-U) through all chord changes
Smooth transition to and from the F chord
Maintaining a relaxed strumming arm and grip
Dynamic control for verse vs. chorus contrast
metronomeWork: Practice strumming pattern on muted strings at 70 BPM, increase to 102 BPM
Use metronome on beats 1 and 3 to establish steady half-time feel
Practice chord changes with metronome at 80 BPM (1 chord per measure)
Play the full song cycle with metronome at 102 BPM
Try playing without metronome and then check your tempo with a metronome to test internal clock
